clinicalPearls: The classic triad is a supranuclear upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upward saccades, and light-near dissociation of the pupils
Pupils are typically mid-dilated and react poorly to light but constrict on convergence (light-near dissociation)
Lid retraction (Collier sign) and impaired convergence or accommodation may accompany the gaze findings
Convergence-retraction nystagmus is best elicited with a downward-rotating optokinetic drum, provoking co-contraction of horizontal recti
In children the commonest cause is a pineal region tumour, and in young adults demyelination or hydrocephalus
In older patients midbrain infarction and hydrocephalus with dilation of the third ventricle are frequent causes
Downgaze is usually preserved early, distinguishing it from progressive supranuclear palsy where downgaze is prominently affected
reference.pathophysiology: The dorsal midbrain and pretectal region contain the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and the posterior commissure fibres that mediate vertical gaze, together with the pretectal olivary nuclei serving the pupillary light reflex. Compression or damage here abolishes voluntary upgaze, disrupts the light reflex pathway while sparing the near response, and disinhibits vergence pathways producing convergence-retraction movements. Causes include pineal and tectal tumours compressing the region, obstructive hydrocephalus dilating the aqueduct and third ventricle, midbrain infarction, and demyelination.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive supranuclear palsy with vertical gaze failure
Congenital or physiological limitation of upgaze in the elderly
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain focused on the pineal region and dorsal midbrain
Imaging assessment of the ventricular system for hydrocephalus
Serum and cerebrospinal fluid tumour markers when a pineal germ cell tumour is suspected
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis where demyelination or infiltration is possible
Pupillary testing to document light-near dissociation
Vascular workup in older patients with an acute presentation
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus requiring urgent neurosurgical assessment
A pineal or tectal mass on imaging needing prompt oncological and surgical evaluation
Rapidly progressive gaze failure with headache and papilloedema
New reduced consciousness suggesting acute aqueduct obstruction
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends entirely on the cause; relief of hydrocephalus or treatment of a tumour can improve the eye signs, while some patients retain a chronic upgaze limitation and pupillary abnormality.
pitfalls: Confusing the syndrome with progressive supranuclear palsy, which characteristically affects downgaze
Missing early hydrocephalus that is treatable if recognised
Overlooking light-near dissociation because pupil testing is not performed in the near
Attributing upgaze limitation in the elderly solely to ageing and failing to image
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
